title: H2 Physics (9478) Paper 3, November 2026: outlook and findings
scope: Analysis and findings only. No question lists or per-question picks. Specimen papers by topic label and marks only.
method: Both papers as one pool: commonness is judged over Papers 2 and 3 together; Paper-3-only reasoning ("rare in Paper 3") is not used.
Topic chances are conditioned on the topic's 2026 Paper 2 status (tested or not), from A-level 2016-2025 (10 pairs) and the 16 school pairs of 2026, blended 0.6 A-level / 0.4 schools.

"In Paper 3 at all" = 4 or more marks anywhere in Paper 3. "Whole Section A question" = the topic leads (has the most marks in) a Section A question of 5 or more marks; the headline band runs from a stricter count by an independent checker (the topic itself has 5 or more marks) up to this count. "Leads a Section B option" = the topic leads an option and has 8 or more of its marks.
Expected Section A marks (of 55): mean Section A marks over sittings with the same Paper 2 status, blended, scaled to 55; mechanics conditioned on Paper 2 mechanics of 21 or more marks.

Within-topic question-type weights: all 188 papers (A-level 2016-2025 Papers 2 and 3; school prelims 2022-2025, 9749 syllabus; school prelims 2026, 9478), every part including data-based questions, parts outside 9478 dropped, a part's marks split equally over its types; each source's share inside the topic blended 0.5 A-level / 0.25 prelims 2022-2025 / 0.25 prelims 2026. New 9478 content (no marks possible in old-syllabus papers) takes its share from the 2026 papers.
The 2026 Paper 3 view of a topic removes the question types the 2026 Paper 2 tested and renormalises the rest.
Checks: an independent rebuild with sensitivity runs, a critic, a syllabus check and a review of the final figures.

section_b.definition: A topic leads an option when it has the most marks in the option and 8 or more of them; conditioned on the topic's 2026 Paper 2 status; blend 0.6 A-level, 0.4 schools 2026. Section B rates come from Paper 3 history (Paper 2 has no 20-mark option).

section_b.specimen_9478_labels_only: Specimen Paper 3 Section B: Q8 oscillations 13 + EM induction 6 + EM forces 2; Q9 nuclear 20 (topic labels and marks only; a weak signal).
section_b.advice: Take nuclear and oscillations to full 20-mark depth, plus one more area: charged particles in E and B fields, or capacitors and RC. You answer only one option, so one strong option is enough on the day.

mechanics: 2026 Paper 2 mechanics was about 31 marks (circular motion 11, the data-based question about 20); the most in any A-level Paper 2 from 2016 to 2025 was 23.
Sittings with 21 or more mechanics marks in Paper 2: Paper 3 Section A had a general mechanics question in Cambridge 1 of 3 and schools 5 of 7. With a cut-off of 18: 4 of 7 and 8 of 10.

So about an even chance of one 8-11 mark mechanics question, on a chapter Paper 2 skipped. In those sittings the untested chapters led as follows: forces and moments 6 times, collisions 3, projectiles 2.
Expected about 7 marks of mechanics in Section A (5-9), against about 12 when Paper 2 has less mechanics.
About a 15-20% chance that a Section B option is mechanics (collisions 13%, projectiles 7%). Cambridge did this in 2020 after a mechanics-heavy Paper 2: a 20-mark collisions option.

Projectile motion: about a 1-in-5 chance of a whole question, usually mixing a launch calculation and air resistance; the two whole Cambridge Paper 3 projectile questions (2017, 2019) were mainly air resistance.
Circular motion has no separate question after this Paper 2, but it is used inside orbits and r = mv/Bq.
structure_and_patterns: Paper 3 (9478): 2 hours, 75 marks. Section A: 55 marks of structured questions, all compulsory (the specimen has 7 questions of 5-11 marks). Section B: 20 marks, one of two questions.

Section A in the 26 Paper 3s analysed (A-level 2016-2025 and 16 schools 2026): 5-8 questions, mostly 7, of 3-14 marks. When a topic comes up in Section A it is usually one question of about 8-10 marks.

Papers 2 and 3 are one pool: a topic can sit in either paper. A one-question topic (nuclear, thermal, EM forces, electric fields, gravitation, oscillations, EM induction) with no question of its own in Paper 2 was in Paper 3 44 times out of 45 (A-level 2017-2025); one with its own Paper 2 question, 8 of 18.

Repeats after Paper 2 (whole question in Paper 2 and again in Paper 3 Section A): single-idea topics almost never come back (oscillations 0/8, EM induction 0/8, circular motion 0/4, thermal 1/10, forces 1/15); many-part topics about 1 time in 3 (quantum 6/16, superposition 5/15, nuclear 5/13, gravitation 5/11, circuits 5/14).

When a Paper 2 topic came back in Paper 3, only about 12% of its Paper 3 marks repeated a Paper 2 question type (62 cases). Parts Paper 2 tested are low, not zero: Paper 3 keeps about 55-70% of their normal rate.
Schools 2026 repeat 23% of their Paper 2 topics in Paper 3; Cambridge (A-level 2016-2025) 36%.

Whole question (lead, 5+ marks) in either paper, 26 sittings: oscillations 26/26, circuits 26/26, superposition 25/26, nuclear 25/26, gravitation 24/26, quantum 24/26, EM induction 24/26, forces 22/26, electric fields 19/26, EM forces 19/26, currents 16/26, projectiles 14/26, collisions 14/26.

Merged questions let one question cover two untested chapters: velocity selector (electric fields + EM forces), capacitor in a circuit (electric fields + circuits), orbit (gravitation + circular motion), a.c. (currents + EM induction), nuclear recoil (nuclear + collisions).

First 9478 sitting: Paper 2 showcased the particle in a box; capacitance and RC are the main new content still untested. In the 2026 school papers, capacitors and RC are about 40% of the d.c. circuits marks and capacitance about 22% of the electric fields marks (see the ★ types). The 9749 years cannot contain them, so shares pooled with those years understate them; here their share is taken from the 2026 papers.
9478 Section A is 55 marks (9749: 60), so the untested topics compete for one fewer slot.
9478 keeps only the threshold-frequency argument of the photoelectric effect.
A-level 2016 is the 9646 format (Section A 40 marks; Section B two of three): weight it down or leave it out.
Electricity and magnetism together: about 20 of the 55 expected Section A marks (19-21.5 in every check).

robust: Electricity and magnetism about 20 of 55 Section A marks (19-21.5 in every check)
Gravitation, oscillations and nuclear about 5-6 expected Section A marks each
The order: electricity first; then oscillations, gravitation, nuclear; the topics Paper 2 used heavily drop
fragile: The mechanics total (5.4-8.9, depends on the source weight and the heavy-Paper-2 cut-off) and the split inside it (forces 0.8-3.6)
Thermal (1.8-3.1; range 0-4): Cambridge 2 of 3 sittings with the same status against schools 0 of 8
Currents: 5.3 rests on 2 Cambridge sittings (2 of 2) against schools 5 of 11; at a lead threshold of 5 it is 3.4
Section B percentages: each rests on 5-13 sittings and on the definition of "leads an option"
Exact Section B pair: 1 in 3 from 8 sittings; forecasters gave 20-40%

effort_rule: Floor first: every topic with about a 1-in-3 or higher chance of a whole question gets to "can do a standard question", in order of importance, before any topic gets deep work.
Cheap insurance: one pass each of collisions, projectile motion, the untested quantum parts, thermal leftovers, wave motion and measurement (uncertainty).

Section B depth: nuclear and oscillations to full 20-mark depth, plus one electricity area (charged particles in E and B fields, or capacitors and RC). That set covers at least one option about 2 times in 3, and more after this Paper 2.
Then the remaining time by expected marks.
Decide effort by the chance of a whole question (questions are lumpy, about 8 marks) as well as expected marks; never argue "rare in Paper 3" for a topic that may simply have sat in Paper 2.

Damped oscillation: explain the decay of amplitude and energy, and calculate the energy lost or the power dissipated
Graphical analysis of oscillator data: determine ω, k or g from a gradient (a–x, T²–m, T²–L), linearise or log–log, or test a proposed relation from read-off values
Define and use the oscillation terms: amplitude, period, frequency, angular frequency, phase, phase difference; express T in terms of f and ω
Energy against time and the kinetic–potential interchange
Speed and acceleration at a given displacement
Describe an experimental method to investigate an oscillator (measure the period or obtain x–t data accurately)
Forced oscillation and resonance: state what is meant and explain the observation
Phase, phase constant and phase difference between oscillations
Frequency response curve and the effect of damping on resonance
Resonant frequency: identify it (peak of the response curve = natural frequency of the free oscillation) and use the resonance condition to find an unknown
Free oscillation: state what it means, define natural frequency, describe a simple example and distinguish it from damped and forced oscillation
Damped-oscillation data: test or use exponential decay of the amplitude (constant ratio of successive amplitudes, ln A against t linear) and extract the damping constant
Predict how the amplitude of a forced oscillation changes when the driver or the driven system changes
Explain why critical (or near-critical) damping is used in a car suspension or similar system
Vertical spring-mass system with gravity: equilibrium extension, amplitude about the equilibrium position, and whether the motion stays s.h.m.
Practical examples of forced oscillation and resonance: useful cases and cases to avoid
Inverse square law for a point source (I = P/4πr²; I ∝ 1/r², A ∝ 1/r): calculate, compare distances, explain and state assumptions
Recall and use v = fλ (with f = 1/T and time = distance/speed)
Malus' law for one polariser (I = I0 cos²θ, A = A0 cos θ): transmitted fraction, or the angle for a given fraction
Polarisation: what it is, why only transverse waves, direction of polarisation
Malus' law through two or more filters (polarised or unpolarised incident light) and the graph of transmitted intensity (or amplitude) against the angle of a rotated filter
Intensity ∝ (amplitude)²: ratios in either direction (A → I and I → A), incl. a rescaled trace
Distinguish transverse and longitudinal waves; classify a given wave
Intensity as power per unit area (I = P/A): define, received power for a given area, gradient of a power–area graph
Read or draw a wave's displacement (pressure)–distance or –time graph and combine with v = fλ
Phase difference between two points of a wave: Δφ = 2πx/λ from a snapshot, from stated numbers, or to locate a point with a given lag
Deduce v = fλ from the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength
Longitudinal (sound) waves on graphs: compressions, rarefactions, pressure–displacement relation, and what a transverse-looking representation shows
Energy is transferred by a progressive wave without transfer of matter
Non-point sources: plane waves (constant intensity) and cylindrical / circular waves (I ∝ 1/r, A ∝ 1/√r)
Sketch displacement–time of a particle (or the profile a time later) from a wave snapshot
Define / explain the wave terms (displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, wavelength, speed, phase, phase difference, wavefront)
Direction (and magnitude) of motion of particles from a wave snapshot
What oscillates: mechanical waves (particles of a medium) vs electromagnetic waves (E and B fields)
Shortest time for a point to reach a given state (zero displacement, crest) from a snapshot
Explain why intensity ∝ (amplitude)² (∝ A²f²) from the energy of the oscillating particles
Single-slit diffraction: b sinθ = λ for the first minimum, central-maximum width, sketching the intensity pattern, and explaining the pattern
Resultant amplitude or phase difference at a point from path-difference geometry
Young's double slit: use ax/D = λ
Diffraction grating: a sinθ = nλ for angles, wavelength, line density or screen positions
Stationary wave: define it, state the conditions for one to form, and explain its formation by reflection in a given set-up
Standing waves in air columns: harmonics of open and closed pipes, N/A positions, and what the envelope represents
Coherence and the conditions for observable two-source interference

Phase, amplitude and spacing of points on a standing wave: read them off a given pattern, relate them to the two component progressive waves, or sketch the amplitude or intensity envelope on a scaled grid
Fringe intensities when the two waves have unequal amplitudes (I ∝ A²)
Wavelength and wave speed from detector readings of a standing wave between a source and a reflector
Double-slit (or multi-slit) fringes modulated by the single-slit envelope: unequal maxima, missing orders, fringes within the central maximum
Diffraction qualitatively: define, draw emerging wavefronts, gap versus wavelength, sound around corners and edges
Limiting angle of resolution and minimum resolvable separation; improving resolving power
State the principle of superposition and apply it to overlapping waves or pulses (including zero resultant when waves meet π out of phase)
State the Rayleigh criterion and represent just-resolved, resolved and unresolved images
Highest observable order and total number of maxima for a grating
Effect of a change on double-slit fringes: separation, brightness, contrast, shift
Grating with white light or two wavelengths: spectra, overlapping and coincident orders
Compare standing and progressive waves (state differences; explain why a standing wave transfers no net energy)
Explain how a grating or double slit produces bright and dark fringes (diffraction at each slit, superposition, path difference)
Two coherent sources and a moving detector: describe how the received amplitude varies, infer source phase, count maxima and minima along a line
Pressure versus displacement nodes and antinodes in a sound standing wave
Interference between direct and reflected waves from one source
Standing waves on a stretched string: draw the mode, label nodes, explain why only certain frequencies, harmonic wavelengths and frequencies
Resonance tube: wavelength, speed of sound and end correction from successive resonance lengths
Separating two close wavelengths with a grating: best order and angular separation against a stated minimum
Describe the use of a diffraction grating to determine a wavelength; choice of order and accuracy
Compare single-slit, double-slit and grating patterns
Two-source interference pattern from a wavefront (ripple-tank) diagram
Apply the first law ΔU = Q + W to a single process (isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, adiabatic) or to a non-gas system, with the signs of Q and W
Ideal gas equation for a single state: find n, N, mass, volume, density or number density
Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas: why U ∝ T, U = (3/2)NkT = (3/2)nRT = (3/2)pV, and ΔU from ΔT or Δ(pV)
Work done by and on a gas expanding or compressed at constant pressure: W = pΔV with sign
Energy to heat a body or change its phase (Q = mcΔθ, Q = ml) from a heater, a given energy or converted kinetic energy, and what the temperature rise means for the device
Mean translational kinetic energy ∝ thermodynamic temperature: ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT
Kinetic-theory assumptions: state them (often the one relating to a named feature) and link each to the model
Heat capacity of a gas at constant volume and at constant pressure: find c (or molar C) from the heat supplied, use given c_v / c_p, and explain why more heat is needed at constant pressure
State what is meant by the internal energy of a system (or of an ideal gas), and use the microscopic KE + PE decomposition
Root-mean-square speed: c_rms = √(3kT/m) and its mass and temperature scaling
Celsius–kelvin conversion and temperature intervals
Fixed amount of gas changing state: combined gas law (Boyle, Charles, pressure law)
Complete a first-law table (Q, W, ΔU) for each stage of a multi-stage process or cycle
Mole, Avogadro constant and Nk = nR: counting particles and switching between molar and particle forms
Explain gas pressure (and changes in it) from the random motion of particles
Derive pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ from a one-dimensional collision model
Cyclic process from a closed p–V loop: net work (enclosed area), direction, ΔU = 0 and net heat
State the first law of thermodynamics in words, and the meaning and sign of each term in ΔU = Q + W
Estimate particle volume or mean spacing from the volume per particle, and use it to judge the kinetic-theory size/separation assumption
Method of mixtures: energy lost by the hotter part = energy gained by the colder part, including melting ice and the final temperature
Electrical determination of specific latent heat (fusion with a control funnel; vaporisation with two heating rates; heat gained from or lost to surroundings)
Thermal equilibrium: define it, describe how it is reached, and judge whether two bodies are in it
Sketch or interpret thermodynamic processes on a p–V graph (isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, adiabatic) using isotherms
First law applied to a change of phase at atmospheric pressure: work against (or by) the atmosphere from ΔV, then ΔU = ml − pΔV (per kg or per molecule)
Gas added or removed: change in amount from two states
Ideal gas: definition by the equation of state, and when a real gas approximates it
Use pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ (p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩, p = ⅔(N/V)⟨E_k⟩)
Ideal-gas graphs: sketch or read p–V, p–1/V, V–T, p–T and pV–T
Explain why the temperature stays constant during melting or boiling although energy is being supplied
Thermodynamic temperature as a measure of the mean microscopic kinetic energy of the particles
Internal energy as a function of state: same final state gives the same internal energy; ΔU path-independent, W and Q path-dependent
Work done as the area under a p–V graph (non-constant pressure)
Mean, mean-square and r.m.s. speed (and mean velocity) of gas particles
Electrical determination of specific heat capacity (solid block; continuous-flow method with two runs to eliminate heat loss)
Cooling effect of evaporation, and how evaporation differs from boiling
Explain atmospheric escape of light gases using r.m.s. speed and the spread of molecular speeds
Define heat capacity, specific heat capacity and specific latent heat (fusion, vaporisation), with units
Heat engine energy accounting per cycle: work output, heat rejected, power and fuel use
Connected or partitioned gas systems: common pressure, conserved total amount
Compare the particles of a substance in two phases at the same temperature: motion, spacing, forces, microscopic KE and PE, internal energy
Thermodynamic scale: absolute zero and independence of any substance
Temperature–time (or temperature–energy) heating curve at constant power: identify phases, find c and l from gradients and plateaus
Explain why the specific latent heat of vaporisation is greater than the specific latent heat of fusion
Empirical temperature scales: temperature from a thermometric property by interpolation, and why scales disagree
Zeroth law of thermodynamics: state it and use it (thermometers)
Unfamiliar kinetic-theory model with a supplied expression (molecular flux, leak or effusion rate)
Energy stored in a capacitor: area under the V–Q graph, U = ½QV = ½Q²/C = ½CV², and energy change when V changes

Field strength as negative potential gradient: E (magnitude and direction) from a V–x graph, E = 0 at turning points, signs and sizes of two charges from their combined V–x graph, and whether E or V can be zero between two charges
Charged particle accelerated or decelerated along a uniform field: speed after a p.d., stopping distance, energy in eV
Deflection of a charged particle projected perpendicular to a uniform field: time in field, vertical displacement, exit angle, screen deflection
Uniform field between parallel plates: E = V/d, potential at a point between plates, force qE and work done by the field
Electric potential due to point charges: algebraic sum, zero-potential point, charge from a V–r value, testing V ∝ 1/r
Capacitance: definition, C = Q/V, charge on the plates and from a Q–V graph
Coulomb force between point charges (and charged bodies treated as point charges): magnitude and direction, resultant from several charges, and the acceleration it produces
Electric field strength of point charges: E = Q/(4πε0r²), resultant field by vector addition, neutral points, and E = F/q
Compare electric and gravitational fields (point sources and uniform fields): similarities, differences, relative magnitudes
Energy conservation for a charged particle moving in a non-uniform field: speed at a point, minimum energy to reach a point or to escape (potential barrier)
Sketch E–x and V–x graphs: point charges, pairs of charges or spheres, parallel plates, and E–x from a given V–x
Charged particle held stationary (or at terminal speed) in a uniform field: balancing qE against weight (and drag)
Charged-particle beam devices: explain why the gun or tube is evacuated, why the beam has a spread of speeds, and the design choices (geometry, p.d.) of a device described in a passage
Describe and explain the path of a charged particle in (and beyond) a uniform electric field
Electric potential energy of a system of charges and work done in moving a charge: U = Q1Q2/(4πε0r), U = qV, W_ext = qΔV

Describe and explain the motion of a charged particle in a non-uniform (radial or two-charge) field: direction from the sign of the charge, acceleration changing with the field strength, speed rising at a changing rate
Define electric potential (and electric potential energy, the electron-volt): the external-force, positive-test-charge wording
Charge sharing between capacitors connected together: charge conservation, common p.d., energy loss
Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium: zero field inside, equipotential surface, charge sharing between connected spheres
Electric field-line and equipotential patterns for combined sources and conductors: unequal or opposite charges, two charged spheres, conductor surfaces
Energy supplied by the source versus energy stored when charging a capacitor: half dissipated
Force from an electric potential-energy function: F = −dU/dr, equilibrium separation and binding energy from U(r)
Charged particle in a circular orbit under Coulomb attraction (electron round a nucleus): speed, kinetic, potential and total energy
Equilibrium of a charged body under the electric force, its weight and a tension (suspended charged sphere)
Capacitance of an isolated charged conductor (sphere or dome): C = 4πε0R from C = Q/V and V = Q/(4πε0R)
Changing an isolated charged capacitor (plates pulled apart): charge constant, new p.d., work done = change in stored energy
Sinusoidal r.m.s.–peak conversions and mean power in a resistor (I_rms = I0/√2, V_rms = V0/√2, ⟨P⟩ = ½P0)
Electrical power P = VI = I²R = V²/R: single components and ratings, cost of energy, power ratios in series/parallel, and cost-based arguments
Drift velocity, number density or current from I = nAvq (n from density and molar mass, from a carrier count, or given; series sections; effect of changing the wire)
Instantaneous power in a resistive load: P = P0 sin²ωt and its P–t graph
Represent a sinusoidal a.c. by x = x0 sin ωt: write the equation, find instantaneous values, and show V and I in phase for a resistor
Mean and r.m.s. values of non-sinusoidal waveforms (square, asymmetric square, rectified, ramp) by the I²–t method
Define p.d. and e.m.f. and distinguish them using energy considerations
Explain half-wave rectification by a single diode and sketch the output p.d. across the load
State what is meant by the r.m.s. value by reference to the heating effect, and why r.m.s. (not the mean) measures the heating effect of an a.c.
Charge, current and number of charge carriers from I = Q/t (incl. direction of conventional current)
Energy transferred from V = W/Q (W = QV, W = VIt)
Deduce that the mean power in a resistive load is half the peak power
Read period, frequency, peak (and peak-to-peak) values from an a.c. waveform; identify a.c. vs d.c.
Derive I = nAvq for a current-carrying conductor
Explain electron motion in a conductor: random thermal motion vs drift, and why a lamp lights almost instantly despite slow drift
Power transmission through resistive cables: p.d. at load, power lost, efficiency and why high voltage is used
Current waveform and r.m.s. reading in a diode-resistor network on an a.c. supply
RC calculations with x = x0 e^(−t/τ) and x = x0(1 − e^(−t/τ)), τ = RC
E.m.f., internal resistance and terminal p.d. (E = I(R + r), V = E − Ir)
Series and parallel combinations: equivalent resistance and the current/p.d. in each resistor
Effective capacitance of a capacitor network (series and parallel)
Sensor potential divider with an LDR or NTC thermistor
Capacitor in a d.c. resistor network: steady state and switching between charge and discharge paths
Resistivity calculation with R = ρ l / A
Describe and sketch the variation of V, Q and I with time for an RC circuit charging or discharging
Charge on, p.d. across and energy stored in each capacitor of a series/parallel network on a d.c. supply
Explain the temperature dependence of resistivity: metals (drift velocity) vs semiconductors/NTC thermistors (number density)
Power delivered to an external load and the maximum power condition (R = r)
Qualitative circuit reasoning: predict how currents, p.d.s, meter readings or lamp brightness change after a change or fault, or diagnose the fault from readings
Resistance at a point on a non-linear I–V graph (V/I, not inverse gradient)
Potential divider output: formula and range with a fixed or variable resistor
Define resistance and apply V = IR to a component
Use the I–V characteristics of two components combined in series or parallel to find the operating current, p.d.s or combined characteristic
Scaling of resistance with geometry (proportionality reasoning, constant-volume stretching)
Data analysis of an RC discharge: area under I–t, τ from graph, ln-linearisation
Draw or interpret a circuit diagram with standard symbols (incl. LDR, thermistor, diode, capacitor)
Sketch and interpret I–V characteristics (ohmic resistor, filament lamp, diode, NTC thermistor)
Potential at a point and p.d. between two points in a divider or bridge (earthed reference)
Loading effect: a voltmeter or load connected across part of a divider
Equivalent resistance of a network by labelling equipotential points and redrawing
Charged particle in uniform circular motion in B: r = mv/Bq solved for radius, speed, KE, momentum, B or mass; period independent of speed; comparing and sketching paths
Magnetic flux density from B = μ0I/2πd, B = μ0NI/2r, B = μ0nI: calculate, scale and sketch it, and judge a solenoid design
Force on a current-carrying conductor: F = BIL sin θ with direction by Fleming's left-hand rule (uniform field, the field of another current, loops, rods in equilibrium, a.c.)
Velocity selector calculations: v = E/B, E = V/d, and the required field directions
Explain why a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform B follows a circular path at constant speed
Helical and non-uniform-field paths: velocity component along B — radius, period, pitch, and describing or explaining the path
Define magnetic flux density and the tesla; express the tesla in base units
Forces between parallel current-carrying conductors: explain them and predict their direction; calculate F/L = μ0I1I2/2πd and the resultant force on a loop or one of several wires
Explain velocity selection with crossed (perpendicular) E and B fields and predict what happens to other particles
Sketch magnetic field-line patterns for a long straight wire, flat circular coil, long solenoid (and permanent magnets)
Current balance and balance-reading methods: measure B (or I, or mass) from moments or from the change in a balance reading
Direction of the magnetic force on a moving charge (Fleming's LHR with sign of charge); deducing charge sign or field direction
Resultant magnetic flux density from two or more currents (vector superposition, null points)
Torque on a rectangular coil in a uniform field (motor / moving-coil meter): τ = NBIA cos θ
Particle accelerators (cyclotron; ring accelerator): E-field acceleration at a gap, B-field steering, dee timing independent of speed, exit energy
Mass spectrometer: velocity selector then semicircle, r ∝ m/q, separation of isotopes
MRI scanner in a data-based passage: Larmor/RF frequency from a stem-supplied ω₀ = γB₀, role of the gradient coils, contrast from relaxation times, practical hazards and limitations
Magnetic field as a field of force: define it, compare it with gravitational and electric fields, and state which fields act on moving/stationary, charged/uncharged particles
Hall effect in a current-carrying slab: deflection of the carriers, polarity of the faces, build-up to the steady state qE = Bqv, the Hall p.d. V_H = Bvd (= BI/(nqt)), and its use as a field probe
Magnitude of the force on a moving charge F = Bqv sin θ, and its link to F = BIL (charge carriers in a wire)
Accelerated through a p.d., then deflected in B: r in terms of V, B and specific charge; scaling with q/m
Effect of a ferrous (soft-iron) core on a solenoid's field; electromagnets and relays
Compare deflection of charged beams in uniform electric vs magnetic fields; identify the field or particle from the path
Specific charge of the electron (Thomson-type experiment): e/m from crossed fields and accelerating p.d.
Faraday's law from a graph: e.m.f. and current from the gradient of a B–t, NΦ–t or solenoid-current graph, instants of zero/maximum e.m.f., and the sketch of the resulting E–t or I–t
State Faraday's law and Lenz's law
Explain the principle of operation of an iron-core transformer (why an alternating e.m.f. is induced in the secondary, why it is smaller/larger) and the meaning of 'ideal'
Ideal transformer calculations (turns ratio, voltages, currents, power), often with r.m.s./peak conversion
Use Faraday's law to explain why an e.m.f. (and current) is induced in a coil: switching a primary (momentary, then zero), a continuously changing field, or a loop leaving a field
Determine the direction of the induced current using Lenz's law (pole argument or force argument)
Straight conductor moving across a field: E = BLv (length inside the field), alternating e.m.f. of an oscillating wire, cancellation in a folded wire, current, retarding force and power
Coil or frame moving into, through and out of a field region: e.m.f., current and direction at each stage, with Φ–t and E–t sketches
Lenz's law as a consequence of conservation of energy (work against the magnetic force becomes electrical energy and heat)
Flux and flux linkage for a coil at an angle to B, and the change in flux linkage when it is rotated, flipped or removed
Energy losses in a real transformer and the design features that reduce them
Average induced e.m.f. from a change in flux linkage over a time interval
Define magnetic flux, magnetic flux linkage and the weber
Explain a practical application of electromagnetic induction (wireless charger, induction cooker, guitar pick-up, metal detector, generator) and the conditions it needs
Eddy-current damping and braking: explain the retarding force, the effect of slots, and energy dissipation
Back e.m.f. in a motor: origin, current at switch-on and at speed, and mechanical power developed
Magnet moving through or past a coil: sketch flux linkage and e.m.f. against time and explain the shape
Rotating coil (a.c. generator): sketch NΦ and E against time with coil orientations and explain the phase relation
Infer the laws of induction from a magnet-and-coil (galvanometer) experiment; e.m.f. vs current
A.c. generator calculations: ω, peak e.m.f. NBAω, peak current, and E(t), I(t) expressions
Predict and explain the effect of changing a parameter on the induced e.m.f. (amplitude, frequency, peak, duration, delay)
Polarity of a moving conductor: which end is at higher potential, from the force on its free electrons
Conductor on rails or falling through a field with no driving force other than gravity (or an initial push): free-body diagram, terminal velocity or decay to rest
Rotating disc (Faraday disc / homopolar generator): E = ½Br²ω = BAf
Change in flux linkage from the area under an E–t graph; search-coil measurement of B (and charge Q = Δ(NΦ)/R)
Photon as a quantum: state what a photon is and calculate photon energy E = hf = hc/λ (J ↔ eV, spectrum region)

Photoelectric evidence for the particulate (photon) nature, and not the wave nature, of e.m. radiation: threshold frequency (meaning, emission or not for a given radiation, f0 = Φ/h), one photon–one electron; interference/diffraction as evidence of the wave nature

Transitions on a given energy-level diagram: photon energy/wavelength (hf = E_upper − E_lower), longest/shortest wavelength, identify and mark a transition, count spectral lines, ionisation energy, series
Energy levels of a particle in an infinite well, E_n = h²n²/8mL²: derive, calculate ground state and level spacing, scaling with m and L
Particle in a 1-D infinite square well: standing-wave solutions ψ_n (boundary conditions, L = nλ/2), sketches of ψ_n and |ψ_n|², superposition explanation
Normalisation constant for square (constant) and sinusoidal wavefunctions from 'area under |ψ|² = 1'
de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p: of a moving particle, of a particle accelerated through a p.d., or given kinetic energy
Distinguish emission and absorption line spectra: appearance, how each is produced, and why absorption lines are dark
Explain how line spectra provide evidence for discrete electron energy levels in isolated atoms (and the electron-wavefunction picture of those levels)
Photon momentum p = E/c = h/λ: calculate it and explain how a massless photon carries momentum
Photon emitted or absorbed in a transition between particle-in-a-box levels: photon energy/wavelength, region, or well width from an observed wavelength (quantum dots)
Excitation by photon absorption vs by particle (electron) collision: which transitions occur for a given photon or electron energy; accelerating p.d. range

X-ray tube and X-ray imaging in a data-based question with stem-supplied models: attenuation ratios (∝ Z³), I = I0e^(−μx) and half-value thickness, transmitted fractions through layered tissue and image contrast, contrast media, scatter blur and patient dose, tube design
Rate of photon emission or arrival from beam power or intensity (P = (dN/dt)·hf)
Force or pressure exerted by a photon beam on an absorbing or reflecting surface (rate of change of photon momentum)

Electron diffraction as evidence for the wave nature of particles: explain the ring pattern from a graphite film (or the spread through a slit), the condition λ ~ atomic spacing, and the effect of changing the accelerating p.d.
Recoil of an atom or nucleus that emits (or absorbs) a photon: conservation of momentum with photon momentum
Interpret a wavefunction: |ψ|² as probability density, most probable positions, probability in a region (area under |ψ|²) or in a small interval (|ψ|²δx), mean vs most probable position

Photon–electron (Compton) scattering, stem-supplied: momentum conservation with photon momentum fixes the outgoing paths; the photon loses energy so its wavelength increases; electron energy and momentum from the energy loss
Uncertainty principle applied to particles passing through a narrow slit: Δy ≈ slit width b, transverse momentum spread Δp ≈ h/b, angular spread θ ≈ λ/b (link to single-slit diffraction)

Single-particle double-slit experiment as evidence for the wave nature of particles: describe the build-up of the fringe pattern from individual localised arrivals (electrons or photons sent one at a time)
Heisenberg uncertainty ΔxΔp ≳ h: minimum uncertainty in position or momentum/velocity from given data (incl. percentage uncertainty in speed, photon Δλ)
Confinement and the uncertainty principle: why a particle in a box has non-zero minimum energy and no definite momentum; estimates of ground-state energy or atom size
Explain the uncertainty principle: a localised particle needs a spread of momenta (wave-packet picture), a definite momentum means no localisation, and the limit is fundamental, not instrumental

Superposition of a single particle's wavefunction in the double-slit experiment: ψ_total = ψ1 + ψ2, probability density |ψ1 + ψ2|², and the pattern with one slit closed or the slits blocked alternately
Admissible wavefunctions: state the conditions a wavefunction must satisfy (normalisable, single-valued, continuous and smoothly varying; zero where the particle cannot be) and judge given sketches
Energy released (Q) in a nuclear reaction from masses or from binding energies
Exponential decay and half-life calculations (x = x0 e^(−λt), (½)^n)
Activity and decay constant: definitions (λ as the probability of decay per unit time), A = λN, number of nuclei from mass or from activity
Nuclear equations and conservation in nuclear processes: balancing, identifying the unknown particle, decay series, gamma emission and neutron activation
Mass defect and nuclear binding energy (and per nucleon) of a nuclide
Rutherford α-scattering: observations, conclusions and trajectories
Why fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy (binding energy per nucleon); definitions and the conditions for fusion
Mass–energy equivalence: E = mc² conversions, rest energy, pair production threshold
Sharing of released energy and momentum among the products of a decay or reaction (two-body share; effect of daughter recoil and of an accompanying gamma photon)
Half-life / decay constant from experimental count-rate data (best-fit curve or ln C–t line)
Spontaneous and random nature of decay: meaning of radioactive decay, evidence and consequences
Distance of closest approach of an α-particle (or other charged particle) fired head-on at a nucleus, by energy conservation (KE → U_E = Qq/4πε0r)
Hazards of ionising radiation: danger by emission type and route of exposure, by half-life, and safe handling
Prediction of the (anti)neutrino from conservation of energy and momentum in β decay
Scale-up: energy from a mass of nuclear fuel, fuel needed for a given power output
Sketch the exponential decay curve and mark half-lives
Binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number: sketch and interpret
Radioactive dating: carbon-14 from the living ratio and measured activity, and parent : daughter ratios
Power or energy output of a radioactive source from activity × energy per decay
Applications of radioactivity: choosing a source by emission type (penetration, ionisation) and by half-life
Nature and properties of α, β and γ radiation (identification, penetration, ionisation, deflection)
Order-of-magnitude nuclear size and density estimates (R = R0 A^(1/3); nuclear vs atomic scale)
Nuclide notation, nucleon vs proton number, isotopes and the unified atomic mass unit

Fission-product yield curve (percentage yield against nucleon number on a logarithmic axis): read the most probable fragment masses and yields, explain the log scale and the equal yields of complementary fragments
Background radiation: origin, measurement and correction

Two-nuclide systems: a radioactive daughter in a decay chain (growth then decay, formation rate against decay rate, which nuclide dominates) and a mixture of two independent nuclides (total activity as a sum of two exponentials)
Fission chain reaction: neutrons released by one fission induce further fissions; control (moderator, control rods) and uncontrolled growth
Coulomb repulsion between protons at nuclear separations and the need for a short-range attractive nuclear force

raw.pairs_doc: Per sitting (A-level 2016-2025: AL<year>; 2026 school pairs: JC<school>): [Paper 2, Paper 3]. Paper 2: S = structured questions, D = data-based question. Paper 3: S = Section A, B = Section B. Values are marks per topic code (a part shared by two topics is split). The 2026 school pairs are 9478 papers; A-level 2016-2025 are 9749 (2016: 9646).
raw.block_budget_doc: Per sitting: Paper 2 marks and Paper 3 Section A / B marks for blocks of topics (MECH = all mechanics chapters; EM = electricity and magnetism; MODERN = quantum and nuclear); "fit" = means and straight-line fits of Paper 3 marks on Paper 2 marks, per source.
